beats.narration_text: Kumusta. This is Liam, in for Bear, with chapter six of INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about one risk score and two audits that disagreed. When base rates differ, a score cannot be calibrated and make equal errors at once. You'll watch forty people counted two ways. The trap: assuming one audit got the arithmetic wrong.

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: ProPublica said the risk score was biased. Its maker said it was fair. How can both be right?
lines: When base rates differ, one score can't be calibrated and make equal errors.
Watch forty people counted two ways: by score box, then by outcome.
The trap: assuming one audit got the arithmetic wrong.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Every fairness audit divides by something, and the headline never says what. Read one audit, and you judge a tool on half the arithmetic. Ask for cleaner data, and you wait forever, because this is a theorem, not a data problem. And it unlocks reading two opposite audits and saying exactly what each one measured.

beats.narration_text: Four terms you'll hear. Base rate: the share of a group who actually reoffend. Calibrated: a score that means the same chance in every group. False positive rate: of the people who never reoffend, the share flagged high risk. False negative rate: of the people who do reoffend, the share called low risk. The misses.

learn.question: Two audits of the same tool reached opposite verdicts. Which one is wrong?
learn.action: Point both headlines at the same forty people.
learn.observation: Same tool, same people, opposite verdicts.
learn.inference: If the data is shared, the disagreement must be in the arithmetic — or in what each audit counts.
learn.next_question: What do the people actually look like, group by group?

beats.narration_text: One risk score, used by courts in Broward County, Florida. In 2016 ProPublica audited it: Black defendants who never reoffended were flagged high risk more often than white defendants who never reoffended. Biased. The maker, Northpointe, audited the same tool: within each score, the same share reoffended in both groups. Fair. Same tool, same people, opposite verdicts. Somebody's arithmetic is wrong. Right?

shot.visual_intent: Forty grey dots in two rows at the bottom — the same people; ProPublica's headline lands top-left ('errors fell unevenly' → 'biased'), an ink line drops from it to the dots; Northpointe's headline lands top-right ('each score meant the same' → 'fair'), its line drops to the same dots; a terracotta dot beside the caption's question 'which one is wrong?'.

show.event: ProPublica headline + its line to the dots on 'biased'
Northpointe headline + its line to the same dots on 'fair'
caption 'which one is wrong?' with the dot

shot.motion_claim: Two verdicts drawn onto one set of dots: the HOOK's dots are the persistent object for the whole section.

learn.question: What does a calibrated score do to one group of twenty?
learn.action: Mark the six who reoffend; sort the twenty into high and low boxes.
learn.observation: High box: 3 of 5 reoffend (60%). Low box: 3 of 15 (20%).
learn.inference: A score's box has a share; that share is what 'the score means' for this group.
learn.next_question: Does the same score mean the same thing in a group with a different base rate?

beats.narration_text: Let's build a small version we can count. Group one: twenty people. Six of them will reoffend. That's a base rate of thirty percent, the chapter's number. Dark dots reoffend; grey dots don't. Now the score sorts them into two boxes. Five land in high risk, and three of those five reoffend: sixty percent. Fifteen land in low, and three of them reoffend: twenty percent.

shot.visual_intent: The headlines clear; group one's twenty dots slide into the left panel; six darken to ink (reoffend); header 'group 1 · base rate 30%'; two box outlines draw ('high', 'low'); the dots sort into them — 5 high (3 ink), 15 low (3 ink); readouts '60%' and '20%' land right of the boxes; a terracotta dot beside '60%'; small dim caption 'constructed · 20 per group'.

show.event: twenty dots into the left panel
six darken on 'six of them will reoffend'
boxes draw; dots sort into high / low
'60%' and '20%' land on the spoken shares

shot.motion_claim: First instance: the base rate is a count of dark dots; the score is a sort into boxes; the box share is readable.

learn.question: Does the same score mean the same thing when the base rate is 50%?
learn.action: Sort group two with the same rule; read each box.
learn.observation: High: 9 of 15 = 60%; low: 1 of 5 = 20% — exactly group one's shares.
learn.inference: The score is calibrated in both groups; Northpointe's audit is correct.
learn.next_question: So ProPublica's audit must be the one with the error?

beats.narration_text: Group two: twenty people, and ten reoffend. Fifty percent. Same score, same boxes. Fifteen land in high, and nine of them reoffend: sixty percent. Five land in low; one reoffends: twenty percent. Look across. High means sixty percent in both groups. Low means twenty in both. That's Northpointe's audit, and it passes.

shot.visual_intent: Group two's twenty dots (waiting as a ghost row in the right panel) darken ten to ink; header 'group 2 · base rate 50%'; its boxes draw and the dots sort — 15 high (9 ink), 5 low (1 ink); readouts '60%' / '20%'; a thin ink line joins the two '60%' readouts across the panels and 'Northpointe: calibrated' lands beneath with a terracotta dot.

show.event: line across the two 60s; 'Northpointe: calibrated' + dot

shot.motion_claim: Second instance: vary one parameter (the base rate), replay the sort; the box shares come out identical.

learn.question: Did ProPublica make an arithmetic error?
learn.action: Recount their way on the same dots: keep only the never-reoffended; count how many sit in high.
learn.observation: 2 of 14 in group one, 6 of 10 in group two — a real gap from the same data.
learn.inference: Both audits compute correctly on identical data; the disagreement is not an error.
learn.next_question: Then what is different between the two counts?

beats.narration_text: So ProPublica must have fudged it. Let's redo their count on these same dots. Their question starts from the grey dots, the people who never reoffended. Group one has fourteen, and two of them sit in the high box. Group two has ten, and six sit in high. Two in fourteen, against six in ten. The arithmetic is clean. Nobody fudged anything.

shot.visual_intent: 'fudged?' writes under the ProPublica label; the dark dots in both panels fade to ghost so only the grey dots remain; the grey dots in each high box pulse; readouts 'flagged, never reoffended: 2 of 14' (left) and '6 of 10' (right) land under the boxes; 'fudged?' gets a terracotta X beside it.

show.event: dark dots fade — only the never-reoffended remain
'2 of 14' / '6 of 10' land on the spoken counts

shot.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn walked to its end on screen: the recount reproduces ProPublica's gap from the same dots — no error to find.

learn.question: What is different between the two counts?
learn.action: Apply Northpointe's filter (a box), then ProPublica's (an outcome), then the misses.
learn.observation: The same dots give equal box shares and unequal outcome shares.
learn.inference: The audits divide by different things; each can be right about its own denominator.
learn.next_question: Can one score satisfy both denominators at once?

beats.narration_text: Here's the reframe. Same dots, two filters. Northpointe's filter: look inside one box and ask what share reoffended. The denominator is the box. ProPublica's filter: look at one outcome, the people who never reoffended, and ask what share got flagged. The denominator is the outcome. And the misses split the same way: three of six in group one, one of ten in group two.

shot.visual_intent: The ghosted dark dots return; Northpointe's filter: the low boxes dim and a bracket-free ink underline marks the high boxes, '60% · 60%' holds; then ProPublica's filter: dark dots ghost again, '2 of 14 · 6 of 10' holds; then the misses: grey dots ghost, the dark dots in the low boxes stay — 'misses: 3 of 6' / '1 of 10' land; a small legend 'box ÷ vs outcome ÷' writes; one terracotta dot beside 'the denominator'.

show.event: Northpointe filter: low boxes dim; high boxes read 60 · 60
ProPublica filter: only the never-reoffended; 2 of 14 · 6 of 10
all dots back; three readouts stand

shot.motion_claim: The representation: one set of dots read through two filters — divide by the box, or divide by the outcome.

learn.question: Holding calibration, can the false positive rates also be equal?
learn.action: Draw both rates as bars; hold the picture.
learn.observation: The viewer commits: yes, no, or only with a better model.
learn.inference: A committed prediction turns the next move into evidence.
learn.next_question: Try it: what happens when we push group two's false positives down?

beats.narration_text: Before anything moves, commit. Keep high meaning sixty percent in both groups. Can you also make the two false positive rates match? Yes? No? Only with a better model? Pick one.

shot.visual_intent: Everything holds; a dim guide line marks group one's '2 of 14' level on a small rate bar under each panel; the question 'hold 60% — equal false positives too?' writes at the bottom; a terracotta dot beside it; nothing else moves.

show.event: the two false-positive bars draw: 2/14 and 6/10
dot beside the question; HOLD on 'pick one'

shot.motion_claim: The predict-before-reveal beat: both constraints on screen, the answer withheld.

learn.question: What happens to calibration when we push group two's false positives down?
learn.action: Move group two's flagged never-reoffended dots from high to low, one at a time.
learn.observation: False positives 6/10 → 2/10; the high box's share 60% → 82%; the low box's 20% → 11%.
learn.inference: With these base rates, the move that equalizes errors is the move that breaks calibration.
learn.next_question: Is that just this repair, or is it forced?

beats.narration_text: Try it. To cut group two's false positives, move its grey dots out of the high box. One. Two. Three. Four. ProPublica's gap nearly closes: two in ten, against two in fourteen. And the high box? Nine of eleven reoffend. Eighty-two percent. Every dot that closes one gap opens the other.

shot.visual_intent: Group two's four flagged grey dots walk, one at a time, from the high box down into the low box; group two's false-positive bar shrinks 6/10 → 2/10 toward group one's 2/14 guide, while the high box's readout climbs 60% → 64% → 69% → 75% → 82% and the low box's 20% drops to 11%; the Northpointe line across the two high readouts breaks (an X beside it, terracotta).

show.event: four dots moved; FP bar at 2 of 10
high readout lands at 82% on 'eighty-two percent'
the 60–60 line breaks; X on 'calibration just broke'

shot.motion_claim: The aha is the morph: the same four dots carry ProPublica's gap closed and Northpointe's gap opened, in one motion.

learn.question: Is the break forced, or just this repair?
learn.action: Write the chapter's identity; plug in both groups at v = 60%.
learn.observation: t/f must be 3.5 in group one and 1.5 in group two.
learn.inference: With v held equal and base rates unequal, the error-rate ratio must differ — equal error rates cannot hold.
learn.next_question: Read the line: what is each piece, and is there any way out?

beats.narration_text: Is that just a bad repair, or is it forced? The chapter gives one line. For each group: v over one minus v equals p over one minus p, times t over f. v is Northpointe's sixty percent. f is ProPublica's number. p is the base rate. Lock v in both groups, and group one needs t over f of three and a half; group two, one and a half. The base rate forces it. Calibration and equal error rates cannot coexist when base rates differ.

shot.visual_intent: The panels shrink and dim into the upper corners; the identity writes in MathTex at centre; each symbol gets its referent beside it ('Northpointe's 60%' under v, 'base rate' under p, 'ProPublica's' under f); the two groups' plug-ins write beneath: 1.5 = 3/7 · 3.5 and 1.5 = 1 · 1.5; the name lands: 'calibration + equal errors: impossible when base rates differ'; a terracotta dot beside it.

show.event: v, f, p get their referents
the name lands, with the dot

shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as the name for what the dots did: the base rate locks t/f once v is locked.

learn.question: What is each piece of the line, and is there a way out?
learn.action: Name the five zones; write the two escapes.
learn.observation: Only the base rate is outside both audits' control; the escapes are equal base rates or a perfect score.
learn.inference: Short of those, no model and no data set satisfies both audits.
learn.next_question: So — back to the two headlines.

beats.narration_text: Read the line. Left: Northpointe's number, as odds. First factor: the base rate, as odds. Neither audit chose it; the world handed it over. Second factor, t over f: how hard the high flag leans toward the people who reoffend. ProPublica's number lives in f. The equals sign is the lock. Fix the left, and the base rate dictates the rest. Two ways out: equal base rates, or a perfect score.

shot.visual_intent: Split stage: the identity persists on the left; five zones write into the right band — 'left: Northpointe's number, as odds' · 'p/(1−p): the base rate — nobody chose it' · 't/f: how hard the flag leans' · 'f: ProPublica's number' · '=: the lock'; then the two escapes write under the equation: p_a = p_b, or t = 1, f = 0; a terracotta dot beside 'the lock'.

show.event: zone 5: the lock, with the dot

shot.motion_claim: The tangent explains the symbols (never derives): the equation stays on the main side, the zones fill the side band.

learn.question: So which audit was wrong?
learn.action: Put each audit's number back under its headline.
learn.observation: Both numbers are correct on the same dots.
learn.inference: Both audits were right; with unequal base rates their fairness definitions cannot both hold.

beats.narration_text: Back to the two headlines. ProPublica: two in fourteen against six in ten. Correct. Northpointe: sixty percent in both high boxes. Correct. Both audits were right, because they divided by different things, and base rates of thirty and fifty percent guarantee those two things can't both be equal. Not a data-quality problem. A theorem. Not taught here: which one to hold, and that the recorded outcome was re-arrest, not crime.

shot.visual_intent: The original forty dots and both headlines return (the HOOK's objects); under ProPublica '2 of 14 · 6 of 10' and a check; under Northpointe '60% · 60%' and a check; the question caption from B10 is replaced by 'both right — different denominators'; a terracotta dot beside it; boundary caption: 'not taught: which to hold'.
shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's headlines and dots resolve: both verdicts stand, each with its denominator; the boundary is one dim line.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. ProPublica and Northpointe were both doing correct arithmetic on the same people. Northpointe divided by the score box: high meant the same chance in both groups. ProPublica divided by the outcome: people who never reoffended were flagged at different rates. When base rates differ, thirty against fifty percent, both can't hold. v over one minus v equals p over one minus p, times t over f, locks them apart. It's a theorem, not a data problem. So picking between them is a values claim, not a calculation.

artifactLines: Both audits did correct arithmetic on the same people.
Northpointe divided by the score box: high meant 60% in both groups.
ProPublica divided by the outcome: the never-reoffended were flagged at different rates.
Unequal base rates lock the two apart: a theorem, not a data problem.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: A hypothetical hospital uses a readmission-risk flag. Audit A reports: among patients flagged high risk, 40% are readmitted, in both Group X and Group Y. Audit B reports: among patients who were never readmitted, Group Y was flagged twice as often as Group X. Group X's readmission base rate is 20%; Group Y's is 40%. Using v over one minus v equals p over one minus p, times t over f, decide whether both audits can be correct at the same time. Then say what each audit divided by, and name one fact you would need before calling the flag biased. Two things to look for. Did it name each audit's denominator, the flagged patients or the never-readmitted ones, before judging either? And did it use the base rates, twenty and forty percent, before calling anyone wrong?
